Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of additions does not change the result: adding a to b and then adding c is equivalent to adding a to the sum of b and c. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result usually must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Since different groupings create different intermediate values, they can incur different rounding errors and produce different final results.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. Suppose a large positive number and a small number are added first. The small number may fall below the available precision and be lost entirely. If that small number is instead combined with another small number before being added to the large number, their accumulated value may be large enough to affect the result. Cancellation between nearly equal positive and negative values can amplify these differences further. IEEE 754 specifies floating-point formats and rounding behavior, but it does not make addition associative.

Large matrix multiplications repeatedly compute dot products. Each output element is a sum of many products, so its value depends not only on the products themselves but also on the order in which they are accumulated. A simple implementation may add terms from left to right, while an optimized implementation may split the work into blocks, form partial sums, and combine those sums as a tree. Parallel CPU threads, GPU work groups, vector instructions, and distributed processes can all create different reduction orders. Scheduling decisions may even change the order between runs.

Consequently, two mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications can produce results that differ in their low-order bits. Those small differences can become more noticeable for long dot products, poorly conditioned data, severe cancellation, or algorithms in which later computations amplify earlier errors. Fused multiply-add instructions can introduce another difference because they compute a product and addition with a single rounding rather than rounding the product separately.

This does not normally mean that one result is fundamentally wrong; both may lie within reasonable numerical error bounds. It does mean that bit-for-bit reproducibility cannot be assumed merely because the inputs and mathematical formula are identical. Reproducibility requires controlling the reduction order, instruction choices, compiler transformations, and sometimes thread scheduling. More robust approaches include deterministic reduction trees, higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or specialized reproducible summation methods. These measures generally impose costs in performance, memory use, or implementation complexity, creating a tradeoff between maximum speed and exact repeatability.
